rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and turns the missing data into a useful constraint, especially in “Bumble's AI relaunch will be judged on one number it hasn't reported yet.” B has some bones, but it keeps reaching for stories it cannot prove: “Users Push Back as Dating Apps Embrace AI Matchmaking” is a category-trend pitch built from one company's update and a vague user-criticism note. A is tighter, more defensible, and more useful to a founder who has to pitch this without stepping on a rake.
gaps_in_A: “the first product the returned founder has put their name on since coming back this year” overstates the update; the facts say the relaunch is under the returning founder-CEO, not that it is her first product or first big move.

“Bumble says women still message first. Now the AI can write the message.” is a sharper headline than the fact allows; the update says the feature helps users write opening messages, not that it writes them outright.
“funding-mechanics” is the wrong story-type label for a public-company markets angle. The substance works, but the label sounds like a finance template got lost in the dating-app aisle.
gaps_in_B: “Users Push Back as Dating Apps Embrace AI Matchmaking” invents a category trend. The update gives Bumble and “some users,” not dating apps plural embracing AI.
“Bumble is the highest-profile dating platform to deploy AI matchmaking and AI-assisted message writing at scale” is unsupported and exactly the kind of confident extra fact that gets a pitch killed.
“If AI Writes the First Message, Is Bumble's Women-First Model Still Feminist?” smuggles in “feminist” and “AI writes” when the update only gives women-message-first and AI help writing openers.
“The relaunch is the stated answer to the subscriber slide” goes beyond the facts. The relaunch follows declining paying users; the update does not say Bumble framed it as the answer.
